title: Amazon EC2 and Amazon RDS service disruption, US East (EBS re-mirroring storm)
mechanisms: automatic EBS re-mirroring (re-replication); re-mirroring search with insufficient back-off; control-plane API timeout policy
evidence_quote_1: Because the EBS control plane (and the create volume API in particular) was configured with a long time-out period, these slow API calls began to back up and resulted in thread starvation in the EBS control plane.
evidence_quote_2: the nodes failing to find new nodes did not back off aggressively enough when they could not find space, but instead, continued to search repeatedly.
notes: Trigger: incorrect manual traffic shift. Re-mirroring storm (redistributive recovery action) exhausted capacity; long timeouts turned it into regional thread starvation.

title: Amazon SimpleDB service disruption, US East
mechanisms: lock-service failure detection / de-registration; handshake timeout + retry; node self-removal from cluster
evidence_quote_1: the server failure pattern in this event resulted in a sudden and significant increase in load on the lock service as it rapidly de-registered the failed storage nodes from their respective replication groups.
evidence_quote_2: After several handshake retries and subsequent timeouts, SimpleDB storage and metadata nodes removed themselves from the SimpleDB production cluster
notes: Trigger: power loss to storage nodes. AWS: self-removal after timeouts "increased the scope of the event".

title: Amazon DynamoDB service disruption, US East
mechanisms: membership-request timeout + retry; storage-server self-disqualification from serving
evidence_quote_1: If the storage servers aren't able to retrieve this membership data back within a specific time period, they will retry the membership request and temporarily disqualify themselves from accepting requests.
evidence_quote_2: Unavailable servers continued to retry requests for membership data, maintaining high load on the metadata service.
notes: Borderline on independence: retry and self-disqualification are parts of the same membership-renewal logic (see pass 2).
pass2_note: Retry and self-disqualification are both steps of one membership-renewal routine (independence fails).

title: Pokemon GO on GCLB (SRE Workbook ch. 11, Case Study 1)
mechanisms: load-balancer (GFE) retry of GET requests; client app retry (single immediate retry then constant backoff)
evidence_quote_1: Under this circumstance, the load balancer retried GET requests, adding to the system load.
evidence_quote_2: These error responses served to effectively synchronize client retries, producing a "thundering herd" problem
notes: Two retry layers owned by different parties (Google LB, Niantic client). Remedy included LB admission override and client jitter.

title: Connectivity Issues (presence/sessions)
mechanisms: session-service reconnect to presence (retry); session buffer-and-retransmit queueing
evidence_quote_1: The failure of the individual presence node caused all the Erlang processes living in our session service to attempt a reconnection to the aforementioned presence service.
evidence_quote_2: The events and messages for these connections quickly filled the in-memory buffers of our session servers and caused many of them to run out of memory and fail.
notes: Buffering is a reliability mechanism but outside the codebook class list; borderline (see pass 2). Trigger: CPU soft lockups + split-brain bug.
pass2_note: Session buffering is not in the codebook mechanism class; only one class mechanism (reconnect) remains.

title: Slack's Outage on January 4th 2021
mechanisms: health-check-driven instance replacement; autoscaler (CPU + Apache worker-thread utilization); LB panic mode; retries and circuit breaking
evidence_quote_1: Some of our instances were marked unhealthy by our automation because they couldn't reach the backends that they depended on. Our systems attempted to replace these unhealthy instances with new instances. Secondly, our autoscaling system downscaled our web tier.
evidence_quote_2: We will also reevaluate our health-checking and autoscaling configurations to prevent inadvertently overloading provision-service again
notes: Two capacity actuators (replacement, autoscaling) acted concurrently on instance provisioning; combined 1,200-instance scale-up overloaded provision-service. CPU signal fell because threads waited on the network (signal distortion not caused by a peer mechanism).

title: US-1 Full Service Disruption - Detailed Root Cause Analysis
mechanisms: cache-bypass fallback; client timeout + retry; utilization-based autoscaler
evidence_quote_1: As front-end API nodes stopped receiving timely responses, they retried performing the original queries, and more incoming requests were added to the queue.
evidence_quote_2: The increased number of in-flight requests due to long query times caused increased utilization, causing them to quickly scale to the maximum number of instances.
notes: Retry/in-flight work inflated the autoscaler signal (observation); scale-out 37->100 added DB load (topological). Recovery required manual scale-down to 45. Not from the user-listed vendor set; found via search, primary PDF verified.
pass2_note: Quotes support retries->load->scale-out->DB load as the primary path; signal inflation secondary.

title: AWS service event, US-EAST-1 (internal network congestion)
mechanisms: automated capacity scaling; client connection retry / back-off
evidence_quote_1: an automated activity to scale capacity of one of the AWS services hosted in the main AWS network triggered an unexpected behavior from a large number of clients inside the internal network.
evidence_quote_2: These delays increased latency and errors for services communicating between these networks, resulting in even more connection attempts and retries.
notes: AWS: a latent issue prevented clients from backing off; scaling activity disabled as remediation.

title: Amazon DynamoDB service disruption, US-EAST-1 (NLB phase)
mechanisms: NLB health checks; automatic AZ DNS failover; health-check-triggered instance termination
evidence_quote_1: The alternating health check results increased the load on the health check subsystem, causing it to degrade, resulting in delays in health checks and triggering automatic AZ DNS failover to occur.
evidence_quote_2: For multi-AZ load balancers, this resulted in capacity being taken out of service.
notes: Only the NLB phase qualifies; the DynamoDB DNS race (root trigger) is a single automation defect. AWS remedy: velocity control limiting capacity removed by failover.

title: Behind the Scenes of the 3/25/26 Voice Outage
mechanisms: gateway-driven client reconnect; per-host session-start rate limit; health-based hash-ring placement with secondary/tertiary failover; RPC retries
evidence_quote_1: Because the majority of our instances were not in the ring, healthy instances were accepting additional traffic acting as the secondary and tertiary failover for unhealthy instances.
evidence_quote_2: As these requests arrived, they triggered our start session rate limit that provides backpressure when we have a flood of requests... but that rate limit hadn't yet been re-tuned after the migration.
notes: Trigger: operator-initiated pod resize. Not in the user-listed vendor archives search; found via web search.

title: GitHub availability report: August 2026 (Aug 17 incident)
mechanisms: service-mesh sidecar concurrency limit; autoscaler (scaled on host service); gateway retries; client retries
evidence_quote_1: The core weakness was that our service-mesh sidecar did not scale up, together with our retry behavior, and clients were not bound enough to keep a partial degradation from amplifying into a broader overload.
evidence_quote_2: Correct autoscaling policies so they account for service-mesh sidecar concurrency and capacity, not just the host service.
notes: Observation coding is inferred from the remediation (autoscaler blind to the limiter), not stated as masking.
pass2_note: Observation path (autoscaler blind to sidecar limiter) is inferred from a remediation item, not stated; dropped under strict reading.
